blocks.text: Feature Extraction, Domain Features, Interaction Features, Polynomial Features, Date Features, and Text Features all shared one thing in common, every new feature came from a single row own content, its text, its date, its numbers, considered on its own. Aggregation Features breaks that pattern for the first time in this module, summarizing information across an entire group of related rows, and attaching that summary back onto each individual row within the group.

This topic covers what an aggregation feature genuinely is, classic real examples like average order value per customer, the pandas groupby and transform pattern that computes and broadcasts these features in practice, rolling aggregations for time ordered data, and two genuinely distinct, easy to miss leakage risks specific to this technique that connect directly back to the Data Leakage topic earlier in this course.
1. What an Aggregation Feature Genuinely Is

blocks.alt: What an Aggregation Feature Genuinely Is
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785443140092-799045012.png

An aggregation feature takes many rows that genuinely belong together, every order placed by one customer, every transaction in one store, and summarizes them into a single value, an average, a total, a count, which is then attached back onto every individual row in that same group. A single customer average order value is computed once across all of that customer orders, then copied onto every row belonging to them.

This is a genuinely different kind of feature engineering from everything else covered in this module, it requires looking beyond a single row to its entire group first, before a new feature can even be computed at all.
2. Classic, Real Aggregation Feature Examples
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785443140092-232273050.png

Average order value per customer, computed across every order that customer has genuinely placed, is a classic example, directly extending the RFM style recency, frequency, monetary value pattern first introduced in the Domain Features topic. Total number of orders per customer captures genuine engagement volume in a single number.

Average price per product category summarizes an entire category into one genuine reference value, letting individual products be compared against their own category typical price, rather than against the entire catalog at once, a genuinely more meaningful comparison in many real business contexts.

blocks.text: 3. The groupby and transform Pattern
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785443140361-849717162.png

In pandas, groupby followed by an aggregate function like mean computes the genuine summary value for each group, while transform takes that extra step of broadcasting the result back onto every original row, rather than collapsing the data down to just one row per group. This transform step is genuinely essential, an aggregation feature needs to sit alongside every original row, not replace the dataset with a smaller, grouped one.

This pattern is genuinely the standard, practical way most aggregation features actually get built in real projects, and it is worth knowing well, since it appears constantly across real feature engineering code.
4. A Worked Example
Computing average order value per customer with groupby and transform shows this pattern applied directly, genuinely attaching one summary value back onto every one of that customer own rows.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "customer_id": [101, 101, 102, 102, 102],
    "order_value": [40, 60, 20, 30, 25],
})

df["avg_order_value"] = df.groupby("customer_id")["order_value"].transform("mean")
print(df)

blocks.text: Every row for customer 101 genuinely receives the same average order value, 50, and every row for customer 102 genuinely receives their own average, 25, exactly the broadcast back behavior transform is built to provide.

blocks.title: A practical habit
blocks.content: Use transform, not a plain groupby followed by a merge, whenever the goal is to attach a group level summary back onto every original row. It genuinely keeps the row count unchanged and avoids an easy to make merge mistake.

blocks.text: 5. Rolling Aggregations for Time Ordered Data

blocks.alt: Rolling Aggregations for Time Ordered Data
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785443140362-985075965.png

When rows are genuinely time ordered, exactly the case covered in the Time Series Data topic much earlier in this course, aggregation can be computed over a rolling window instead of the entire group at once, a rolling seven day average order value, for instance, updating as time genuinely moves forward rather than staying fixed across the whole history.

This is a genuinely natural extension of the static aggregation covered above, instead of one single summary value per group, a rolling aggregation produces a genuinely changing value that reflects only the most recent, relevant window of activity.

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: A rolling aggregation is genuinely more informative than a single static one whenever recent behavior matters more than distant history, exactly the kind of recency signal RFM style features are built around.

blocks.text: 6. Leakage Risk One: Future Rows in a Rolling Window

blocks.alt: Leakage Risk One: Future Rows in a Rolling Window
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785443140363-144239545.png

A rolling window must genuinely only include past rows relative to each specific row being computed, never future ones. A rolling average computed carelessly, including rows that come after the current one in time, genuinely commits the exact temporal leakage covered in the Data Leakage topic earlier in this course, letting a feature see information that would not genuinely exist yet at real prediction time.

This is a genuinely easy mistake to make with rolling computations if the window direction is not set up carefully, and it is worth double checking explicitly every time a rolling feature is built on time ordered data.
7. Leakage Risk Two: Aggregating Across the Train Test Split

blocks.alt: Leakage Risk Two: Aggregating Across the Train Test Split
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785443140363-276184633.png

A second, genuinely distinct risk shows up even without any time component at all, computing an aggregation, average order value per customer, for instance, across the entire dataset before splitting it into training and test sets. Doing this genuinely lets test set rows quietly influence the aggregate value attached to training rows for the same customer, exactly the train test contamination covered in the Data Leakage topic.

The fix mirrors that same earlier topic directly, split the data first, then compute every aggregation using only the training set, applying the resulting values to validation and test rows without recomputing them there, respecting the exact discipline covered fully in the Train Validation Test Split topic.

blocks.text: 8. Aggregation Features Versus What Comes Next

blocks.alt: Aggregation Features Versus What Comes Next
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785443140364-458705674.png

Aggregation Features closes out this Feature Engineering module, which opened with Feature Extraction and Domain Features, moved through Interaction and Polynomial Features, went deep on Date and Text Features, and now ends with this genuinely distinct group level technique. Every one of these topics has focused on creating new, more useful features from the raw material this course started building understanding of all the way back in Data Collection and Understanding.

With a genuinely rich, well engineered feature set now in hand, the next module, Feature Scaling, addresses a different, equally practical concern, making sure every one of these features, old and newly engineered alike, sits on a scale that the algorithms covered later in this course can actually work with well.

items: An aggregation feature summarizes a group of related rows into one value, attached back onto every row in that group.
Average order value, total orders, and average price per category are classic, real aggregation features.
The pandas groupby and transform pattern is the standard way to compute and broadcast these features.
A rolling aggregation extends this to time ordered data, updating as time genuinely moves forward.
A rolling window must only use past rows, never future ones, to avoid genuine temporal leakage.
Aggregations must be computed only from the training set, never the full dataset, to avoid train test contamination.
